content: The National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) is a system designed to help countries progressively enhance the availability, quality, and utilization of health workforce data. This is achieved by monitoring a set of standardized indicators that support the achievement of Universal Health Coverage (UHC), Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and other health-related objectives. The NHWA aims to standardize and improve the interoperability of health workforce information systems. The NHWA defines standardized indicators to achieve several goals: Generate reliable information and evidence on human resources for health (HRH). Enable effective planning, implementation, and monitoring of workforce policies to advance UHC. Improve the comparability of health workforce data at national and global levels. Engaging in the NHWA allows countries to better understand the characteristics of their health workforce, including its size and distribution. It strengthens HRH information systems to routinely produce high-quality data and evidence, which can guide policy decisions tailored to the country’s needs. This includes collaboration with ministries of health, education, and finance, as well as professional associations, training institutions, and academia. The NHWA also informs priority investments needed to strengthen the health workforce and supports UHC. Additionally, it enhances the comprehensiveness, quality, and comparability of HRH data over time, fosters cross-country collaboration in data collection, and facilitates the documentation and sharing of experiences and best practices. The NHWA is relevant at national, regional, and global levels. It enables countries to collect, analyze, and utilize health workforce data to develop evidence-based policies and plans. This supports global monitoring efforts, including those related to the SDGs, UHC, and other global health commitments. For example, the NHWA includes specific indicators on health workforce density and distribution, which are critical for addressing imbalances and shortages. The World Health Organization (WHO) and its partners developed the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 (GSHRH) to accelerate progress toward UHC and the SDGs. This strategy emphasizes equitable access to health workers within strengthened health systems. Member States are urged to improve HRH data and evidence, report annually to the Global Health Observatory, and progressively implement the NHWA. The strategy also recommends harmonized metrics and methodologies to strengthen health workforce data, information, and accountability. At the country level, the NHWA can address key HRH challenges, such as imbalanced geographic distribution, workforce shortages, migration, evolving workforce demographics, and inadequate regulations. It can also optimize planning by answering critical policy questions, such as how to allocate resources more effectively, monitor and address health workforce migration, and improve workforce retention in underserved areas. The NHWA aligns closely with the health labor market framework for UHC, which provides a comprehensive view of health labor market domains, including education, labor market dynamics, financing, governance, policies, and regulation. This framework addresses key areas such as policies on health worker production, inflows and outflows (e.g., migration and re-entry into the workforce), maldistribution, inefficiencies, and private sector regulation. The NHWA Handbook is structured in a modular format aligned with the health labor market framework. It includes 78 health workforce indicators organized into 10 modules covering three main components: education, labor force, and serving population health needs. These modules correspond to the major types of policies required to deliver safe, effective, and person-centered health services. The handbook also provides information on regulation and the status of HRH monitoring and management systems. The implementation of the NHWA is a country-led activity that builds on existing national systems and mechanisms. It aims to progressively improve a country’s capacity to collect, analyze, use, and report health workforce indicators to inform policy-making based on national needs. This collaborative effort involves multiple stakeholders and is supported by WHO’s Implementation Guide, which outlines eight non-sequential steps across three phases: 1. Conceptualization: Establishing political buy-in, multi-sectoral governance, and assessing HRH information quality. 2. Operationalization: Addressing all aspects of data collection, flow, validation, and dissemination under a legal framework. 3. Process Revision: Regularly revising NHWA implementation to account for changes in data availability or stakeholder involvement. To facilitate timely and effective data collection and use, WHO has developed the NHWA Online Data Platform. This platform allows countries to record, analyze, and visualize health workforce information for their own use. Additionally, the NHWA Web Portal displays aggregated, validated data provided by countries. This publicly available portal serves as a global public good, disseminating harmonized health workforce data and contributing to global reports, including the Global Health Observatory. The NHWA was developed through a stepwise process involving extensive consultations with experts from both developed and developing countries. These experts included academics, national HRH and information systems specialists, policy planners, international organization representatives, and health professionals. WHO and its partners have also developed various tools and guidance to support NHWA implementation at the country level.
